lesson.title: Check in with someone you love
lesson.scenario: Lina and Omar catch up at home. Learn a casual check-in, say how you feel, and ask the other person back.

steps.instruction: Lina checks in with Omar. Respond as Omar: you are well.

prompt.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)

answers.rationale: This describes a feminine speaker; you are taking Omar’s role.
This answers the check-in about Omar himself.
This describes the day; the task asks how Omar himself feels.

evaluation.correctExplanation: Ana mnīḥ answers about Omar himself. The lesson’s question is a casual check-in.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.
evaluation.retryHint: Use ana and Omar’s form of “well.”

steps.instruction: You are Lina. After saying you are well, ask Omar the same question back.

answers.rationale: This addresses Lina, but your listener is Omar.
This asks about a third person instead of your listener.
Inta addresses Omar and returns the check-in.

evaluation.correctExplanation: W-inta? invites Omar to answer without repeating the question.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.
evaluation.retryHint: Your listener is Omar: use inta.

steps.instruction: You are checking in with Lina. Choose the question addressed to her.

answers.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Lina)
answers.rationale: ʿĀmle marks the question to Lina.

answers.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)
answers.rationale: ʿĀmel is the form addressed to Omar.

answers.meaning: What did you do today? (to Omar)
answers.rationale: This asks for completed activities and uses masculine address.

evaluation.correctExplanation: Shū ʿāmle? changes the address form for Lina.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.
evaluation.retryHint: Listen for the ending of ʿāmle.

steps.instruction: Answer as Lina: you are a little tired.

prompt.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Lina)

answers.rationale: Ktīr makes the tiredness strong, changing “a little.”
This describes Omar; Lina uses taʿbāne.
The description matches Lina and keeps the degree mild.

evaluation.correctExplanation: Ana taʿbāne shwayy preserves both Lina’s self-description and “a little.”
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.

steps.instruction: Lina asks how you are doing. Respond as Omar: a little tired.

prompt.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)

answers.rationale: This is the feminine self-description, while you are Omar.
This describes Omar with mild tiredness.
This changes the requested degree to “very.”

evaluation.correctExplanation: Ana taʿbān shwayy is Omar’s self-description; shwayy keeps it mild.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.

steps.instruction: Lina offers Omar a rest. Accept and say you want a little rest.

prompt.meaning: Do you want to rest? (to Omar)

answers.meaning: Yes, I want to rest a little.
answers.rationale: Āh accepts; biddi artāḥ expresses the speaker’s wish.
This declines the offer; the task asks you to accept.
This reports completed activities instead of accepting the offer.

evaluation.correctExplanation: Āh, biddi artāḥ shwayy accepts and says what Omar wants now.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.
evaluation.retryHint: Accept first, then say what you want.

steps.instruction: A new check-in: respond as Lina that you are well.

prompt.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Lina)

answers.rationale: This is Omar’s self-description; you are Lina.
This says you are tired, changing the requested meaning.
This describes Lina as well.

evaluation.correctExplanation: Ana mnīḥa changes the self-description to fit Lina in this new exchange.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.

steps.instruction: You are Omar. After answering, return the check-in to Lina.

answers.rationale: This addresses Omar, but Lina is your listener.
Inti addresses Lina and keeps the check-in going.

answers.meaning: Yes, I want to rest a little.
answers.rationale: This asks for rest rather than returning the question.

evaluation.correctExplanation: W-inti? completes the exchange by inviting Lina to answer.
evaluation.incorrectExplanation: Compare the speaker, listener, and intended meaning.

lesson.unitTitle: Everyday conversations with someone you love

introduction.goal: Check in, say how you feel, and keep a short exchange going.

line.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)
Do you want to rest? (to Omar)
Yes, I want to rest a little.

expressions.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)
How are you doing? (casual check-in to Lina)

introduction.usageNote: Check in, answer about yourself, then ask the other person back. Keep the speaker’s description separate from the listener’s address form. In this scene shū ʿāmel functions as a casual check-in; in another context it can ask what someone is doing.
introduction.dialectNote: Urban Palestinian teaching target. The casual check-in choice follows Palestinian-speaker feedback relayed and clarified by the owner on September 30, 2026. No universal claim about every Palestinian greeting is made. Feminine address and composed exchange are AI-assisted drafts; no native-expert review. Keep transliteration available: ʿ = ع; ā/ī/ū are long vowels. Jordanian alternatives are not introduced here.
introduction.recordingNote: No reviewed recordings yet. Six dialogue turns above are the revised script. Keep each speaker/address form and exact transcript; no native-speaker review is claimed. Browser/device speech remains an optional preview.

teachingCards.title: Start with a casual check-in

phrase.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Omar)

teachingCards.note: Lina asks Omar how he is doing. In this greeting, answer about how you feel. When addressing Lina, use shū ʿāmle.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Lina. Greet Omar with a casual check-in.

teachingCards.title: Answer about yourself
teachingCards.note: Ana identifies the speaker. This form describes Omar; Lina says mnīḥa.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Omar. Lina checks in. Tell her you’re well.

teachingCards.title: Give a little detail
teachingCards.note: Lina is describing herself, so taʿbāne has a feminine ending. Shwayy keeps the tiredness mild.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Lina. Tell Omar you’re a little tired.

teachingCards.title: Keep the conversation going
teachingCards.note: You do not need to repeat the whole question. Inti addresses Lina; inta addresses Omar.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Omar. After answering, ask Lina the same question back.

teachingCards.title: Check in with Lina

phrase.meaning: How are you doing? (casual check-in to Lina)

teachingCards.note: The person you address changes the ending: ʿāmel to Omar, ʿāmle to Lina.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Omar. Start a casual check-in with Lina.

teachingCards.title: Offer a little rest

phrase.meaning: Do you want to rest? (to Omar)

teachingCards.note: Biddak asks what Omar wants; biddi says what you yourself want. Keep tirtāḥ with the question and artāḥ with your reply.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Lina. Omar is tired. Ask if he wants to rest.

teachingCards.title: Say what you need

phrase.meaning: Yes, I want to rest a little.

teachingCards.note: Biddi marks what the speaker wants. Reuse shwayy to ask for a little rest.
teachingCards.recallCue: You are Omar. Accept Lina’s offer and say you want to rest a little.
